food.text: The Aghlabid dynasty ruled Ifriqiya, roughly modern Tunisia and nearby lands, from 800 to 909 as vassals of the Abbasid Caliphate. Agriculture and trans-Saharan trade both expanded under their rule, fueling economic growth and a larger urban population. Part of that trade was in people: slaves were obtained through the trans-Saharan trade, through Mediterranean commerce, and from raids on other lands like Sicily and Italy. Some of these slaves were turned into soldiers, and 5,000 black Zanj slaves were recorded as stationed in the garrison at Abbasiya.

The Ibadi Rustamid dynasty ruled for a century and a half from its capital Tahert, in present-day Algeria. This walled stronghold had a fortress, a marketplace and a steady water supply, plus gardens of fruit and vegetables that helped sustain it as a religious and economic center.

In the 10th century, the Muslim scholar Mutahhar ibn Tahir al-Maqdisi described trans-Saharan trade in which food and clothing were carried south into sub-Saharan Africa. In exchange, traders brought back slaves, gold and coconuts to the Maghreb and the wider Islamic world.

After the Fatimids left Ifriqiya for Egypt to found Cairo, their Zirid vassals ruled from Kairouan through an agricultural and commercial heyday. Overseas trade in local farm produce ran high, and the Zirid court became known for its refinement.

art.text: Kairouan was founded in 670 by the Umayyad general Uqba ibn Nafi as the capital of the new province, and its Great Mosque was built the same year. The mosque was enlarged in 724 to four times its original size. It is considered one of the masterpieces of Islamic architecture.

Some of the oldest surviving Islamic-era monuments in the Maghreb are military structures in Ifriqiya. The best known are the Ribat of Sousse and the Ribat of Monastir, dating from the Aghlabid period in the 9th century. Built at intervals along the coast, they could signal each other from afar.

Kairouan and Cordoba were among the most important centers of artistic development in the western Islamic world from the 8th to 10th centuries. Later, the Almoravids and Almohads unified the Maghreb and al-Andalus and helped spread a wider regional style across both.

During the Aghlabid period in the ninth century, Arabic inscriptions carved in Kufic script were used, sparsely but widely, to decorate mosques in Ifriqiya. Vegetal compositions of leaves and stems appeared alongside them, marking the early beginnings of geometrically arranged arabesques later developed further in Islamic art.

Some domes in Ifriqiya from the 9th and 10th centuries are especially accomplished in design and decoration. One is the Aghlabid dome in front of the mihrab in the Great Mosque of Kairouan. The other is the Zirid Qubbat al-Bahw dome in the Al-Zaytuna Mosque in Tunis.

The Idrisids, who arrived at the end of the 8th century, founded the city of Fes as their capital. It became the major political and cultural center of early Islamic Morocco. Immigrants from Tunisia and al-Andalus brought cultural and artistic influences from their homelands.

After the Aghlabids, the Fatimids took over Ifriqiya in the early 10th century and built a heavily fortified new capital at Mahdia, on a narrow peninsula. Its only gate was the Skifa al-Kahla, meaning 'the dark vestibule', with a vaulted passage 44 meters long.
The Aghlabid and Zirid domes of Kairouan and Tunis are elegant ribbed domes. Their stonework flourishes include decorative niches, inscriptions, and shell-shaped squinches.

The Mosque of Agadir was founded in 790 by Idris I. The Mosque of Aghmat, southeast of present-day Marrakesh, was founded in 859 by Wattas Ibn Kardus. Both were hypostyle mosques with prayer halls supported by rows of pillars, and their layouts are known from modern archaeology.
The Qarawiyyin and Andalusiyyin mosques in Fes were founded in the 9th century in hypostyle form. Their structures themselves were rebuilt during later expansions.

Ribats were residential fortresses that guarded the early frontiers of Muslim territory in North Africa. The ones at Sousse and Monastir also contained prayer rooms that acted as mosques. Dating from the same Aghlabid period, the stone city walls of Sousse and Sfax resembled earlier Byzantine-Roman walls in Africa.
The Al-Zaytunah Mosque in Tunis was built around 731 CE by Ubayd Allah ibn al-Habhab. It was the second mosque built in the Maghreb after the Kairouan Mosque.
When the Great Mosque of Kairouan was enlarged in 724, the old structure was demolished except for the mihrab. The new mosque served as a model for all later mosques in the Maghreb.

war.text: Al-Kahina was an Amazigh warrior-queen of the Aurès who united various tribes to resist the Muslim conquest. She defeated Umayyad forces at the Battle of Meskiana and became the uncontested ruler of the whole Maghreb. In September or October 703 she was decisively defeated at the Battle of El Jem; she fled the battlefield, and Hassan pursued her, caught her and killed her near a well in the Aurès Mountains. It is reported that she was beheaded and her head was sent to the Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan in Damascus as proof of her death.

In 740 a Berber revolt against Umayyad Arab rule began in Tangier under Maysara al-Matghari, inspired by Kharijite preachers. It was provoked by Arab tax-collectors: the deputy governor Omar ibn al-Moradi set about seizing Berber property and enslaving people, though alternative accounts say he simply doubled their tribute. The rebels took Tangier and killed the hated governor, then swept down western Morocco killing Umayyad garrisons and local governors, including Ismail ibn Ubayd Allah, the son of the Kairouan emir. It was the first successful secession from the Arab Caliphate, then ruled from Damascus, and it spread across the Maghreb and into Al-Andalus.

The Byzantine Empire used the deposition of Hilderic by his cousin Gelimer as a reason for war against the Vandals. In the Vandalic War of 533 to 534, the general Belisarius made his formal entry into Carthage in October 533, and the city then served as capital of Byzantine North Africa.

In 647 Abdallah ibn Sa'd led 20,000 soldiers from Medina into the Maghreb, swiftly taking Tripolitania. He then defeated a much larger Byzantine army at the Battle of Sufetula, and the Arab troops withdrew after the new Exarch of Africa agreed to pay tribute.

Uqba ibn Nafi was an Arab general who led the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb and is credited with establishing Umayyad rule in North Africa. In Sous al-Adna he met the Berbers in heavy numbers, routed them and killed them extensively, while his cavalry captured women and seized wealth, so that a Byzantine slave girl from there was worth a thousand dinars in the Mashriq. In 683 he was ambushed by the Berber Christian king Kusaila and his Byzantine allies at the Battle of Vescera, and was killed beside his hated rival Abu al-Muhajir Dinar, whom he had earlier bound in iron chains and taken on raids to Sous in chains.

The Berbers ended Umayyad rule in the western Maghreb after the Battle of Badgoura, where by some estimates two-thirds of the Arab army were killed or captured, and the Battle of the Nobles, a massacre of the cream of the Ifriqiyan Arab nobility. The Umayyads won the decisive Battle of al-Asnam, perhaps the bloodiest encounter of the Berber wars, where some 120,000 to 180,000 Berbers are said to have fallen, though historian Khalid Yahya Blankinship calls that number an exaggeration not to be trusted even vaguely. The rebel leader Uqasha was taken prisoner and executed shortly after. After the rebels failed to capture Kairouan, their armies dissolved and the west split into small statelets.

When Hassan ibn al-Nu'man marched into the Aurès Mountains in 698, al-Kahina demolished the city of Baghaya, believing he meant to use it as a fortified base. The armies met in the Meskiana Valley, where she defeated him decisively and pursued him as far as Gabes, and he fled Ifriqiya and stayed in Cyrenaica for five years. Later, believing the Muslims came for the riches of the cities, she was said to have begun a scorched earth campaign. It had little effect on the mountain and desert tribes but lost her the support of the oasis-dwellers, who went to Barqa and asked Hassan for help, and it hastened her defeat.

The Fatimids organized an army from the Kutama of northeastern Algeria, converted to Ismaili Shi'ism by the missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i in 893. After numerous battles against the Aghlabids of Ifriqiya, the Fatimids emerged victorious in 909 and conquered Ifriqiya.

literature.text: Kairouan was founded by the Umayyads around 670, during the reign of Caliph Mu'awiya. It quickly became an important centre for Sunni Islamic scholarship and Quranic learning, attracting Muslims from many parts of the world.

The library of the Great Mosque of Kairouan holds a large collection of calligraphic scrolls and manuscripts, the oldest dating to the second half of the ninth century. Among them are Qur'ans and books on Maliki fiqh, forming the oldest surviving collection of Maliki legal literature.

Jews were among the original settlers of Kairouan, and their community's golden era began in the late eighth century. During this era, Kairouan became a world center of Talmudic and Halakhic scholarship for at least three generations.

The Rustamid dynasty, which ruled from Tahert for a century and a half until 909, produced scholars such as Abd al-Wahhab ibn Abd al-Rahman, who wrote a legal work called Masa'il Nafusah, and Aflah ibn Abd al-Wahhab, who mastered Arabic literature, mathematics and astronomy. Another scholar, Abu al-Yaqzhan ibn Aflah, wrote about 40 works.

Muhammad ibn Hani al-Andalusi al-Azdi, who lived from about 936 to 973, became chief court poet to the Fatimid Caliph al-Mu'izz and wrote poems praising the Fatimids. Many contemporaries and later historians called him al-Mutanabbi of the West. He was murdered at Barqah in Cyrenaica on Wednesday, 30 April, about 973, at the age of 36, while returning to the Maghreb to bring back his family. Accounts of his murder differ.

Among the mosque library's finest works is the Blue Qur'an, produced in the second half of the tenth century, whose suras were written in gold on vellum dyed with indigo. Its verses were separated by silver rosettes, and each surah began with a band of golden stylised foliage.

Because of their intellectual enthusiasm, the Rustamids transferred valuable works from the Mashriq to libraries in the Maghreb, especially al-Ma'shumah in Tahert and Khizanah Nafusah in Jabal Nafusah. This learning gave Tahert a reputation that earned it nicknames including Little Basra.

At the age of 27, Ibn Hani traveled to Africa to serve Jawhar al-Siqilli, a general of the Fatimid ruler, but received only 200 dinars for a qasida written in his honor. He then moved on to al-Masila, where compatriots of his were ruling.

At al-Masila, Ibn Hani was treated with great respect by the rulers Ja'far ibn Ali and Yahya ibn Ali and composed notable poems in their honor. His fame spread so widely for his odes that Caliph al-Mu'izz himself summoned him to serve at the Fatimid court.

When poets of Ifriqiya lampooned Ibn Hani to demoralize him on his arrival, he said he would reply to none of them unless Ali al-Tunusi wrote to him. Ali responded that he would never lampoon him, since Ibn Hani had given him a status above all other poets of the land.

science.text: The Great Mosque of Kairouan hosted a university where scholars taught both Islamic thought and the secular sciences, a role historians compare to that of the University of Paris in medieval Europe. The mosque's fame, together with other holy sites in the city, helped Kairouan grow into a major center of learning in the Maghreb.

The physician and philosopher Isaac Israeli ben Solomon studied natural history, medicine, mathematics, and astronomy, and was reputed to know all the "seven sciences" of his day. He became one of the foremost Jewish scholars in the Arab world, later serving rulers of the Fatimid Dynasty of North Africa.

Hydraulic engineering already had a long tradition in the Maghreb, and many aqueducts and other waterworks from the Roman and Byzantine period survived or were restored during the early Islamic period. This engineering tradition continued under the Aghlabid dynasty, which ruled Ifriqiya during the 9th century and the beginning of the 10th century.

In about 904, Isaac Israeli ben Solomon was nominated court physician to the last Aghlabid prince, Ziyadat Allah III. Between 905 and 907 he traveled to Kairouan, where he studied general medicine under Ishak ibn Amran al-Baghdadi.

In Kairouan, Isaac Israeli ben Solomon's fame grew so widely that Muslim physicians considered his Arabic medical writings "more valuable than gems." His lectures attracted many pupils, most notably Abu Ja'far ibn al-Jazzar and Dunash ibn Tamim.

The Sofra, a large cistern in the center of old Sousse, may have been a pre-Islamic structure restored or rebuilt by the Aghlabid emir Ibrahim II, who ruled from 875 to 902. It has a barrel-vaulted chamber divided by rows of arches on square pillars, with roof openings for adding water and a small round settling tank.

Isaac Israeli ben Solomon was the first physician to write about tracheotomy in Arabic. He advised using a hook to grasp the skin of the neck during the procedure, a technique also earlier described by Paulus of Aegina.

Isaac Israeli ben Solomon later served as physician to 'Ubaid Allah al-Mahdi, founder of the Fatimid Dynasty of North Africa, who reigned from 910 to 934. The caliph enjoyed his physician's wit, especially in exchanges that confounded the Greek physician al-Hubaish.

politics.text: Byzantine rule in North Africa lasted around 175 years. It began in 533/534 when Justinian I reconquered territory that had belonged to the Western Roman Empire. It ended with the conquest of Carthage in 698 and the loss of the last outposts, especially Septem, in 708/711.

The Muslim conquest of the Maghreb took nearly 70 years, making it one of the longest campaigns of the early Muslim conquests. It began in 647, when the Byzantine army was defeated at Sufetula, where the Exarch Gregory was personally slain by Ibn al-Zubayr, and a massive tribute was exacted. It ended in 709, when Caliph al-Walid I took the last Byzantine strongholds.

In 893 an Arab Shia missionary, Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i, arrived from Yemen and converted the Kutama of northeastern Algeria to Ismaili Shi'ism. Under the Fatimid dynasty they raised an army against the Aghlabid dynasty of Ifriqiya. After numerous battles the Fatimids won in 909 and established the Fatimid Caliphate.

Musa ibn Nusayr conquered modern Algeria and Morocco and began the mass recruitment and Islamization of the Berbers on a scale unseen elsewhere. His early campaigns seem to have focused on gaining as much booty as possible, both plunder and especially captives. They also set the stage for the 711 conquest of Iberia.

Al-Kahina was an Amazigh warrior-queen of the Aurès who was both a religious and a military leader. She united Amazigh tribes against the Muslim conquest and ruled a sovereign Berber state from the Aurès Mountains to the oasis of Ghadames from 698 to 703.

Byzantine North Africa was first run with a Praetorian prefect holding the civil powers and a Magister militum per Africam holding the military ones. From 591 at the latest the two were merged into a single office, making the region an exarchate. Emperor Maurice used this bundling and decentralization to counter imperial overstretch.

After a failed military campaign under King Garmul against the Eastern Roman Empire, the Mauro-Roman Kingdom collapsed. Its fall led to several petty Berber kingdoms, including the Christian Berber Kingdom of Altava, which lasted until the Umayyad conquest of the seventh and eighth centuries.

The Sulaymanid dynasty ruled part of western Algeria from 814 to 922. Its founder Sulayman I was the brother of Idris I, who founded the Idrisid dynasty in Fez. Both were sharifs, great-grandchildren of Hasan ibn Ali and so descended from Muhammad.

Abu al-Muhajir Dinar began a pivotal policy of rapprochement with the Berbers, together with their large-scale recruitment. This came in the years after Uqba ibn Nafi founded Qayrawan in 670. The policy helped prepare the way for the later mass conversion of the Berbers.

In 683 Uqba ibn Nafi was ambushed and killed at the Battle of Vescera near Biskra by the Berber leader Kusaila. Kusaila then forced all Arabs to evacuate their just-founded Kairouan and withdraw to Cyrenaica.

The Talkata, a Sanhaja tribe of central Maghreb, dominated the region in the 10th century while allied with the Fatimids. Their first known leader was Menad ibn Manḳūs, whose son Ziri founded their capital, Achir, in 935 and became the ancestor of the Zirid dynasty.

After the Battle of Carthage in 698, Umayyad Arab forces sacked the city and destroyed it in a scorched earth policy, fearing the Byzantine Empire might reconquer it. The city walls were torn down, the water supply cut off, the agricultural land ravaged and the harbours made unusable. In the 8th century its ruins were then used as a source of building materials for Kairouan and Tunis.

In the 10th century, the ancestors of the Beni Guil, an Arab tribe tracing its lineage to the prophet's grandson Hasan ibn Ali, were given the right to graze in eastern and western Morocco. The grant came from the Fatimid ruler Al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah.

Accounts of Al-Kahina's ancestry differ. According to various Muslim sources she was the daughter of Tabat, or of Yanfaq, while Ibn Khaldun called her the daughter of Mātiya ibn Tifan. Her legacy has been retold through oral tradition since her lifetime.

The last recorded ruler of the Kingdom of Altava was Caecilius, called Koceila or Kusaila, meaning "leopard" in Tamazight. In 690 he met Arab reinforcements under Zuhair ibn Kays at the Battle of Mamma, with the support of Byzantine troops. Vastly outnumbered, he was defeated and killed.

Carthage was the seat of the Exarchate of Africa after 590. In the early seventh century its exarch, Heraclius the Elder, rebelled against the Byzantine emperor Phocas. His son Heraclius then succeeded to the imperial throne.

philosophy.text: The Berbers embraced Islam en masse during the Arab conquest of the Maghreb, at first with limited commitment. They kept the religion because its doctrine was clear and simple, and it strongly appealed to them.

Christianity in the Maghreb declined gradually after the Muslim conquest of 647 to 709. The article names constant warfare and persecutions among the causes, along with many Christians migrating to Europe. It still survived for a long time, as sporadic sources document, and by the 15th century Christian Berber communities in Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria had disappeared. Before that, under Roman rule, many Berbers had adopted Christianity and churches had been built across the region.

Early Islamic philosophy began with al-Kindi in the early 9th century, during the period known as the Islamic Golden Age. It included falsafa, which covered philosophy, logic, mathematics and physics, and kalam, a rationalist form of Scholastic theology. The Maghreb belonged to the western part of the Islamic world, where philosophical activity later declined significantly.

From the late fifth and early sixth century, the Maghreb included several Christian Berber kingdoms. Berber Christianity had grown during centuries of Roman rule, when the Church of Carthage played a key role in developing Christian philosophy and theology.

According to al-Mālikī, Al-Kahina travelled with an "idol". Mohamed Talbi and Gabriel Camps read it as a Christian icon, while M'hamed Hassine Fantar saw a Berber deity and traditional Berber religion. The hypothesis that she was a Christian remains the most likely.

culture.text: The Arab Muslim conquerors left a much more lasting influence on the culture of the Maghreb than the conquerors before or after them. By the 11th century the Berbers had become significantly Islamized and Arabized.

Christianity had spread widely among the Berbers under Roman rule, and from the late fifth and early sixth century the region included several Christian Berber kingdoms. After the Muslim conquest of 647 to 709, Christianity slowly declined, with constant warfare and persecutions among the causes. Under the Almohads, the record shows persecutions, and Abd al-Mu'min forced the Christians and Jews of Tunis to convert in 1159. Some communities survived for centuries, but by the 15th century Christian Berber communities in Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria had disappeared.

Al-Kahina, whose name means 'the priestess', was an Amazigh warrior-queen of the Aurès and a religious and military leader. For five years, from 698 to 703, she ruled a sovereign Berber state stretching from the Aurès Mountains to the oasis of Ghadames.
The Berbers embraced Islam en masse during the conquest, at first with limited commitment. They kept to the faith because its doctrine was clear and simple, which strongly appealed to them.

The Donatist sect, named after the Berber Christian bishop Donatus Magnus, rejected any priest, regardless of rank, who submitted to imperial authority. Donatus called for martyrdom in defense of the faith, and his call was especially embraced by the dissatisfied lower classes. It spread mainly among indigenous Berbers, who blended Christianity with many local customs.

In 670 Uqba ibn Nafi founded Qayrawan. Abu al-Muhajir Dinar began a pivotal policy of rapprochement with the Berbers, and later Musa ibn Nusayr began the mass recruitment and Islamization of the Berbers on a scale unseen elsewhere.
Islam reached Morocco in 680 CE, brought by the Arab Umayyad dynasty of Damascus. The first Islamic dynasty to rule Morocco were the Idrissids.

Arab migrants settled in all parts of the Maghreb during the conquest, arriving as peaceful newcomers who were welcomed everywhere. About 150,000 Arabs settled there in the 7th to 8th centuries, and a considerable portion belonged to the Najdi tribe of Banu Tamim.

According to al-Mālikī, Al-Kahina was accompanied in her travels by an 'idol'. Some historians read it as a Christian icon, while the Tunisian historian M'hamed Hassine Fantar held that it was a Berber deity. Her being a Christian remains the most likely hypothesis.

Under early Muslim rule, Jews flourished in major urban centers throughout the Maghreb. Jewish communities developed in cities such as Kairouan and coastal cities of Tunisia, and also in Tlemcen, Béjaïa, Algiers and Fes. Some lived among the Berber populations of the Atlas Mountains.
Al-Kahina's legacy has been retold through oral tradition since her lifetime. One study describes how her legend emerged after several transformations between the 9th and the 14th centuries.
